source_refs.note: Topic 9.3 with Figs. 9.10 to 9.13 (PDF 198-200, printed 195-197). Equation numbers 9.7 and 9.8 are used twice in print; recorded as a finding.

blocks.text: When we place an element of area in an electric field, some of the lines of force pass through it (Fig. 9.10). The number of field lines passing through a certain element of area is known as the electric flux through that area, usually denoted by the Greek letter phi_e. For example, the electric flux through area A in Fig. 9.10 is 4, while the flux through B is 2. To give a quantitative meaning to flux, the field lines are drawn such that the number of field lines passing through a unit area held perpendicular to them at a point represents the intensity E of the field at that point.

blocks.alt: Magenta field lines run upward and spread apart. Near the bottom, where they are close together, a small yellow area A is crossed by 4 lines. Higher up, where they are farther apart, an equal yellow area B is crossed by 2 lines.
blocks.caption: Figure 9.10: Electric flux through a surface normal to E (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 9.10).

blocks.text: Usually the element of area is represented by a vector area A, whose magnitude is equal to the surface area A of the element and whose direction is along the normal to the area.

items: Area A held perpendicular to the field lines (Fig. 9.11a): EA lines pass through it, so phi_e = EA; the flux is maximum.
Area A held parallel to the field lines (Fig. 9.11b): no lines cross the area, so phi_e = 0; the flux is minimum.
Area inclined so that its vector A makes an angle theta with E (Fig. 9.11c): we take the projection of the area perpendicular to the field lines, A cos theta, so phi_e = EA cos theta (9.9).

blocks.alt: Three panels with magenta field arrows E pointing right. (a) Maximum: a green area stands upright across the field and its vector A points right, along E. (b) Minimum: the area lies flat, parallel to the field, and A points straight up. (c) The area is tilted so that A makes an angle theta with E; a yellow dashed strip beside it, labelled A cos theta, is its projection perpendicular to E.
blocks.caption: Figure 9.11: (a) Maximum; (b) Minimum; (c) (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 9.11).

blocks.title: Electric flux
blocks.text: The electric flux through a patch of flat surface in terms of E and A is phi_e = EA cos theta = E.A ... (9.10), where theta is the angle between the field lines and the normal to the area. Electric flux, being a scalar product, is a scalar quantity; its SI unit is N m^2 C^-1.
Electric flux through a surface enclosing a charge

Let us calculate the electric flux through a closed surface in the shape of a sphere of radius r due to a point charge q placed at its centre (Fig. 9.12). To apply phi_e = E.A, the surface should be flat, so the total surface area of the sphere is divided into n small patches with areas of magnitude delta A1, delta A2, ..., delta An, the direction of each vector area being along the outward perpendicular to the patch. The electric intensities at the centres of the patches are E1, E2, ..., En. According to Eq. 9.10, the total flux through the closed surface is phi_e = E1.delta A1 + E2.delta A2 + ... + En.delta An ... (9.11).

blocks.alt: A large shaded sphere with a charge +q at its centre. On a small curved patch Delta A of its surface a black arrow Delta A and a red arrow E both point radially outward.
blocks.caption: Figure 9.12: The total electric flux through the surface of the sphere due to a charge q at its centre is q/ε0 (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 9.12).

blocks.text: The direction of the electric intensity and the vector area is the same at each patch, and |E1| = |E2| = ... = |En| = E = (1/(4 pi eps0)) q/r^2 ... (9.12). Since E is parallel to the vector area, theta = 0 and E.delta A = E delta A cos 0 = E delta A. So phi_e = E (delta A1 + delta A2 + ... + delta An) = E x (total spherical surface area) = (1/(4 pi eps0)) (q/r^2) x 4 pi r^2, which gives phi_e = q/eps0 ... (9.13).

Now imagine a closed surface S enclosing this sphere (Fig. 9.13): the flux through S is the same as that through the sphere. So the total flux through a closed surface does not depend upon the shape or geometry of the closed surface; it depends upon the medium and the charge enclosed.

blocks.alt: An irregular pink closed surface S encloses a pale green sphere with +q at its centre. Straight magenta field lines run outward from +q through both the sphere and S.
blocks.caption: Figure 9.13 (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 9.13).
